title: This Fish Hunts With a Red Searchlight Its Prey Can't See

scenes.text: This fish shines a light its prey can't see.
The stoplight loosejaw lives 500 to 2,000 metres down. Under each eye, an organ glows red.
Down there, most animals have lost the ability to see red. To them, the beam is invisible.
The loosejaw sees it with a chlorophyll-like pigment, believed to come from the copepods it eats. No other animal does this.
Its lower jaw has no floor, just a hinge and a muscle. One of the widest gapes of any fish.
And what does it eat with those fangs? Mostly copepods, smaller than rice grains, hunted with a light they never see.

description:
The stoplight loosejaw (Malacosteus) lives below about 500 metres and carries a large photophore under each eye that emits red light, a colour most deep-sea animals cannot see, so it hunts with an effectively invisible beam.
It is the only animal known to use a chlorophyll derivative to see red, apparently obtained from the copepods that make up most of its diet. Its lower jaw has no skin between the two sides and is about a quarter of its body length.
What would you hunt with an invisible light?
